newsitem.title: UK: Weinstock gives way to Simpson at GEC.
newsitem.headline: Weinstock gives way to Simpson at GEC.

text.p: Lord Arnold Weinstock, one of Britain's best-known industrialists, formally passed his chief executive's job at giant GEC Plc to George Simpson on Friday, but 72-year-old "Arnie" was set to remain on the scene.
Weinstock received a standing ovation from nearly 500 shareholders gathered at the General Electric Company Plc's annual meeting at London's Hilton Hotel.
He has been the group's driving force and chief strategist for 33 years and the company board, individual shareholders and Simpson praised both his track record and his character.
Lord Prior, the GEC chairman, said of him, "No other industrialist in the whole of the post-war period has made a comparable contribution to the survival and the success of British industry."
Prior also described him as having "a brilliant, original mind" that rejected the received wisdom or other people's ideas and questioned all situations and views -- as well as his own.
But shareholders were left in little doubt that Weinstock will continue to make available his advice in his new, so-called "honorary", role as Chairman Emeritus.
A company source said Weinstock wanted to continue going into the office regularly as he feels he has left some of his work unfinished.
"He hopes George will do it, and would like to help him."
In his reply to Prior's testimonial, Weinstock made clear he saw Simpson as a force for continuity, not change, in building up the electronics, engineering and defence combine.
Leadership of GEC, he said, took "teams of people who trust eachother and can work together -- putting ego behind them."
"I think one of the great qualities of George Simpson is exactly that. He won't be striking out on his own...replacing (GEC) with a peculiarly Simpsonian brand of company," he added.
Simpson told reporters his relationship with Weinstock would be on the same friendly basis that it had been in the past, adding, "it'll be good having him around to pick his brains".
He would, he added, take some time to get to know the company and "step into the big man's shoes".
The meeting heard a long justification of Simpson's generous pay, pensions and bonus package from Lord Prior.

The deal had caused such controversy among fund managers and investors that the performance criteria for the new chief executive's bonus scheme had to be toughened up in the last few days to ensure it was approved by institutions.
Shareholders at the meeting approved the package by an overwhelming majority, with only a handful of objecting votes.
Simpson said he felt that some more time could have been spent on defining the performance criteria in the first place, and that he was happy about the revisions.
In another example of his unconventional approach to running GEC, Weinstock will have to be paid a pension direct from company funds rather than from the firm's own pension scheme.
Prior told the meeting that over the years Weinstock had always put off discussing his inclusion in the GEC scheme "because he didn't like the idea of money being spent".
Characteristically, Weinstock could not resist the opportunity of using his final address to shareholders to offer them some words of advice.

He said he was concerned at some of the views that have taken prominence after recent reviews of corporate governance in Britain -- now codified under the Cadbury and Greenbury reports -- and said small investors needed to take care.
"Greenbury and Cadbury are not engraved in stone and brought down from Mount Sinai," he said.
